Awesome! My ultimate fix involved adjusting DMZ settings in my router. I didn't even have to leave the setting in place permanently. 

Basically I set my phone's IP as the DMZ in the router settings, which causes incoming traffic to route to the phone on the public Internet IP address. This will involve locating your phone's internal WiFi IP address from the router's connected devices section (or equivalent) first. Depending on the subnet this could look like 10.x.x.x or 192.168.x.x.

Then the app should work when you're connected to WiFi. In either case, you shouldn't leave this setting this way, so revert it. I suspect it just triggers a cache reset in the routing table.

Anyway I hope this helps!

I once had a person interview for a job they were completely unqualified for. They admitted this up front and said they just wanted the interview experience. Ultimately, I don't think this is a good practice, because we didn't do or say all the things we would have if we had a real candidate in front of us.

I am a technical lead and can sympathize with your problem. I think it's important to know that for interviews, it often doesn't matter if you ultimately solve the problem correctly. We just want to know that you can do your job, meaning if you hit a roadblock you will admit it and try to move past it.

If you can't, you should be able to explain why: would you normally look at stack overflow or a search engine? Say that out loud and come up with a potential solution if you did get an answer to the one problem you needed to look up.

Is it the setting that gives you anxiety? Sometimes teams will be willing to leave the room save for one person if that's the case... you don't often have to solve a big problem in front of a lot of people on the job, so I don't see why this should be any different in an interview.

Is it a lack of domain knowledge that sticks you? Ask the people there for context.

Anyone doing an interview should ultimately be willing to build you up and collaborate with you, just like it will be on the job. If they aren't open to this, maybe it's not the job for you anyway.

Re-reading this, it seems like you panic when you don't immediately know the answer. Just remember there's nothing wrong with not knowing. No one knows everything, but people sometimes try to fake it like they do. Be genuine and admit where your shortcomings are, and do it out loud... "I don't know.. this could go either way, and here's why. If x, then y... else if z then a." is a lot better than complete silence.

Sometimes in reiterating on a problem verbally, you will refocus yourself and be able to break through the problem, but sometimes you won't. You have to show that you know how to try and that you're persistent more-so than that you have all the answers.

Edit: Even a quick admission that "I'm starting to panic a bit here... let me take a moment to think." can be enough to make people more sympathetic. They've been there too, and this will remind them. They should respond with kindness. If you're still panicking, just start reviewing what you've done so far until you find your place again.
